deep.reconstruction:
Context: this folio is a working draft of Art. 5 of Riemann's Göttingen doctoral dissertation, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse' (1851). The draft is close to the printed text. The previous page drafts material on cross-cuts (Querschnitte) and the Dirichlet-type existence conditions. The next page continues into branch points (Windungspunkte): permutation of sheets around a point sigma, cycles of length m, and a 'Windungspunkt (m-1)ter Ordnung'.

Content of the page, in modern terms:

(1) Setting. The variable point O = x+iy is no longer taken to range over the whole plane A. It ranges over a bounded surface T spread over A, i.e. a domain T with a local homeomorphism (projection) pi: T -> A. Riemann explicitly allows T to cover the same part of the plane several times ('aufeinanderliegende Flächen'). He excludes overlying sheets that are joined along a line, which would be a fold ('Umfaltung') or a splitting into two overlying sheets ('Spaltung'). In modern terms, pi is a local homeomorphism away from isolated points; the isolated exceptional points are the branch points treated on the next page. Fold curves, as in non-open maps, are excluded.

(2) Claim. If the boundary of T is given by its position and its orientation (which side is inside and which is outside), then the number of sheets over every part of the plane is determined. This does not, however, determine the surface itself: 'ihr Verlauf kann sich jedoch noch verschieden gestalten', i.e. the connection pattern of the sheets is not fixed.

(3) Proof sketch. Draw any line l through the covered part of the plane and let N(p) be the number of sheets over p. N is locally constant off pi(boundary of T), because folds and splittings are excluded. Crossing the boundary from outside to inside raises N by 1; crossing in the opposite sense lowers it by 1. Since N = 0 far away, N is determined everywhere.

Modern restatement (my formulation): N(p) = deg(pi over p) = wind(pi(boundary of T), p) = (1/(2 pi i)) * contour integral over the boundary of dz/(z-p). This holds for p not on the image of the boundary, with the boundary positively oriented, so that the interior lies to the left.

(4) Crossed-out and continued lines at the bottom. Along a part of l that does not meet the boundary, each sheet adjacent to the 'Ufer' (bank) of l continues in a definite way. Any indeterminacy can occur only at isolated points, either on l itself or at a finite distance from it. So the numbers of adjacent sheets on the two banks are equal. This prepares the permutation-of-sheets argument on the next page, which leads to branch points of order m-1.

No computations appear. The page is conceptual and definitional.
errors: No mathematical errors. The sheet-count rule (+1 crossing inward, -1 crossing outward) is correct given the stated hypotheses: N vanishes outside a bounded region, no folds, and branching only at isolated points.

The argument is a sketch. Local constancy of N off the boundary relies on the excluded folds/splittings and on branch points being isolated; Riemann states these as hypotheses rather than proving anything.
The draft says 'begrenzte Fläche'. The printed version drops 'begrenzte' (the 1851 text reads 'eine über dieselbe ausgebreitete Fläche T'). This is a minor wording change, not an error.

results.what: Concept of a bounded surface spread over the plane, possibly multi-sheeted, with folds and splittings excluded (unbranched/branched covering domain)
results.modern_name: Riemann surface as a (branched) covering domain over the plane; 'Überlagerungsfläche'

results.what: Number of sheets over a point is determined by the oriented boundary: it changes by +1/-1 when crossing the boundary inward/outward
results.modern_name: Sheet number = degree of the projection = winding number of the boundary image around the point (argument principle / degree theory)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851 (Art. 5); later formalised via degree theory (Kronecker, Brouwer)

results.what: Remark that the boundary data do not determine the sheet connections; the local continuation of sheets along a line leads to the permutation of sheets around isolated points (next page: Windungspunkt)
results.modern_name: Monodromy permutation / branch points of a covering

deep.surprise_reason: This is a near-final draft of Art. 5 of Riemann's published 1851 dissertation. The only novelty is in wording variants, e.g. 'begrenzte Fläche' and the crossed-out terms 'Zuspitzungen' and 'Umfaltung', which are of philological rather than mathematical interest.

checkable.asserts: A boundary curve circling the origin twice positively has winding number 2, so a surface bounded by it has 2 sheets over the origin.
For a point outside the boundary circle the winding number, hence the sheet count, is 0.
Reversing the orientation of the boundary (swapping inside and outside) changes the count by sign: winding number -1, matching the -1 rule for crossing outward.

transcription_corrections: 'Wir verstatten diese Ausbreitung[?]' — the word after 'diese' is more likely 'Einkleidung' (the printed text has 'Wir wählen diese Einkleidung, bei der es unanstössig sein wird, von auf einander liegenden Flächen zu reden').

'eine Spaltung in zwei aufeinanderliegende Flächen' — the printed version reads 'Spaltung in auf einander liegende Theile'. The draft appears to have 'Spaltung in zwei aufeinanderliegende Flächen', with 'nicht vorkommt' lost to strike-outs.
The '24' in the right margin is the folio/page number, not part of the text.

Bottom lines are best read, by comparison with the printed Art. 5, as: 'Längs des Ufers dieser Linie setzt sich nun jeder angrenzende Flächentheil auf ganz bestimmte Art fort, so lange die Linie die Begrenzung nicht trifft, da eine Unbestimmtheit ... nur in einem einzelnen Punkte, und also entweder in einem Punkte der Linie selbst oder in einer endlichen Entfernung von derselben stattfinden kann'.
'auf beiden Ufern ... von gleich viel Flächentheilen bedeckt' is consistent with the printed 'deren Anzahl auf jeder Seite gleich ist'.
